about: BIZOMAT Engineering Drafting Knowledge Base, shipped entries. Written for BIZOMAT from general engineering drafting practice. No text of any standard is reproduced; standards are referenced by number and title only. Every shipped entry is a RECOMMENDED practice whose wording has not been checked against the licensed standard text (validation: unverified). Company entries and verified requirements are added by the owner (sw_drafting_feedback, kind guideline).

entries.concept: A drawing communicates requirements, not the 3D model.
entries.explanation: The reader is a machinist, fabricator, inspector or installer. The drawing must let that person make or check the item without asking questions or measuring the model.
entries.practice: Decide the drawing's purpose and reader first; choose views, dimensions and notes for that reader.
entries.example: A fabrication drawing of a frame shows member marks, cut lengths and welds; an installation drawing of the same frame shows only the envelope, fixing points and mass.
entries.correct: One drawing per purpose, each complete for its reader.
entries.mistake: Putting every model dimension on one sheet because the CAD system can.

entries.concept: Orthographic views are placed by a projection method, shown by its symbol.
entries.explanation: In third angle projection the top view is above the front view and the right view to its right; in first angle they are the other way round. The symbol in the title block tells the reader which.
entries.practice: Use the projection the reader expects (third angle in Australia and North America, first angle common in Europe) and always show its symbol.
entries.example: AS 1100 drawings: third angle; a German supplier's drawing: first angle.
entries.correct: Views placed by one method, symbol shown.
entries.mistake: Moving a projected view to a free spot on the sheet so it no longer sits where the projection says.

entries.concept: Use the fewest views that define the item completely.
entries.explanation: Each extra view costs space and reading time and can contradict another. A view earns its place only if it shows something no other view shows clearly.
entries.practice: Plates: one plan view and one edge view. Turned parts: one side view with diameters, an end view only for flats, holes or keyways. Add sections and details instead of extra outside views.
entries.example: A 10 mm plate with holes: a plan view and one edge view are enough; a third view repeats the thickness.
entries.correct: Every view justified by information only it carries.
entries.mistake: Front, top, right and isometric on every part by default.

entries.concept: The main view shows the most characteristic shape, in the working or machining position.
entries.explanation: The reader recognises the part from the main view; other views are read relative to it.
entries.practice: Choose the view that shows most features true shape and the fewest hidden lines; for turned parts the axis horizontal.
entries.example: A shaft is drawn lying along its axis, not end-on.
entries.correct: Main view = the most informative view.
entries.mistake: Taking SOLIDWORKS' Front view as the main view whatever the part's orientation in the model.

entries.concept: A section replaces hidden detail with visible, dimensionable geometry.
entries.explanation: Counterbores, countersinks, blind holes, stepped bores, pockets and internal grooves appear only as hidden lines in outside views; hidden lines should not be dimensioned.
entries.practice: Cut a section through the internal features (through their axes), label it A-A, place it in projection or clearly labelled, and dimension depths in it.
entries.example: A plate with counterbored holes: section A-A through a row of holes shows the counterbore diameter and depth.
entries.correct: Depths of internal features dimensioned in a section.
entries.mistake: Dimensioning a counterbore depth to hidden lines, or omitting the depth.

entries.concept: A detail view enlarges a small feature so it can be dimensioned clearly.
entries.explanation: Grooves, undercuts, small radii and threads are often too small at the sheet scale to carry readable dimensions.
entries.practice: Circle the feature, label it, and draw it at a preferred enlarged scale (2:1, 5:1, 10:1) near its parent view.
entries.example: A retaining-ring groove 1.1 mm wide on a shaft drawn at 1:1: detail B at 5:1.
entries.correct: Small features dimensioned in an enlarged detail.
entries.mistake: Crowding tiny dimensions at the sheet scale.

entries.concept: Dimensions start from the faces that locate the part in use and in the machine.
entries.explanation: A datum scheme (primary, secondary, tertiary) mirrors how the part is held and how it mates. Dimensioning from datums stops tolerances stacking up.
entries.practice: Primary datum: the seating or mounting face. Secondary and tertiary: the faces or holes that locate it. Give feature positions from them (baseline).
entries.example: A machined block: base face A, a long side B, an end face C; every hole position from B and C.
entries.correct: Positions from functional datums, each once.
entries.mistake: Hole-to-hole chains that accumulate error.

entries.concept: Dimension the way the part is made and checked.
entries.explanation: A machinist sets up on a datum, then mills and drills feature by feature. Dimensions that match that order can be used without arithmetic.
entries.practice: Group each feature's size and position in the view that shows it true shape; give depths from the face it is machined from.
entries.example: A pocket: width and length in the plan view, depth from the top face in a section.
entries.correct: No calculation needed to find a position or depth.
entries.mistake: Giving a depth from the bottom face when the feature is machined from the top.

entries.concept: A thread is specified by its designation, not by the tapping drill.
entries.explanation: A plain hole at tapping-drill size in the model does not say the hole is threaded. The drawing must give the thread designation and the full-thread depth; the drill size and depth are the workshop's choice unless they matter.
entries.practice: Confirm with the designer which holes are threaded; specify e.g. M6 with full-thread depth; use a cosmetic thread or Hole Wizard in the model so the callout is associative.
entries.example: Ø5.0 x 15 blind in the model: if it is M6, call out M6 with its thread depth.
entries.correct: Thread designation and depth on the drawing, confirmed.
entries.mistake: Dimensioning Ø5.0 only, so the hole is drilled and never tapped.

entries.concept: A member detail gives everything to cut and drill one member.
entries.explanation: Fabricators work member by member: section designation and grade, cut length, end cuts, hole positions from the member's end and gauge lines, and the member mark.
entries.practice: Draw each member along its length; dimension holes from one end (or the connection's working point) and from the gauge line; list section, grade, length and mark.
entries.example: B12: 200UB25.4 (grade to confirm) x 6000, 4 holes Ø22 each end at the gauge.
entries.correct: One member, one detail, complete.
entries.mistake: Expecting the fabricator to scale hole positions from the general arrangement.

entries.concept: Connections are detailed separately at a larger scale.
entries.explanation: Plates, cleats, stiffeners, bolts and welds at a connection are small relative to the members; they need their own scale and dimensions.
entries.practice: Show the connection with plate sizes, bolt group (number, size, grade, gauge, pitch, edge distances) and weld symbols; reference it from the general arrangement.
entries.example: End plate 220 x 120 x 12 with 4 bolts in two rows: pitch, gauge and edge distances shown.
entries.correct: Bolt group fully dimensioned; bolt grade and category stated by the engineer.
entries.mistake: Choosing a bolt grade from the hole size.

entries.concept: Every member carries a mark that ties the shop drawing to its place in the structure.
entries.explanation: Marks let erectors find each member on the erection drawing; orientation marks stop members being installed reversed.
entries.practice: Give each distinct member a mark; show the marks on the erection or general arrangement drawing.
entries.example: C1 to C8 for columns, B1 to B12 for beams.
entries.correct: A mark on every member, consistent across drawings.
entries.mistake: Identical-looking members with no mark or orientation indicator.

entries.concept: Weld type, size, length and quality are design requirements.
entries.explanation: They come from the designer's calculation and the applicable welding standard, never from the drafter's judgement.
entries.practice: Show each weld with a symbol (type, size, length, all-round, field weld) as specified; state the welding standard and weld category or quality level in the notes.
entries.example: A fillet weld 6 mm both sides, all round, as specified by the engineer.
entries.correct: Every joint has a specified weld, or is marked as not welded.
entries.mistake: Writing 'weld all round' without size, or inventing a size.

entries.concept: A weldment drawing lists every member with section, length, end cuts and quantity.
entries.explanation: The cut list is what the saw operator works from; identical members are grouped under one item.
entries.practice: Use SOLIDWORKS' weldment cut list where possible (it stays associative); balloon each member with its item number.
entries.example: Item 1: SHS 40x40x3 x 500, square ends, qty 2.
entries.correct: Cut list on the drawing, balloons to every member.
entries.mistake: Overall frame dimensions only, leaving cut lengths to be worked out.

entries.concept: Welding distorts; faces that must be accurate are machined after welding.
entries.explanation: Heat input pulls members out of position. Critical mounting faces and bores are left with machining allowance and finished after welding.
entries.practice: Show post-weld machining on a separate drawing or clearly marked views, with datums on the machined faces; state any fabrication sequence the designer requires.
entries.example: A gearbox mounting frame: weld, stress relieve if specified, then machine the mounting pads flat and drill.
entries.correct: Machined-after-welding features clearly identified.
entries.mistake: Tight tolerances on as-welded faces.

entries.concept: A sheet-metal part is cut from its flat pattern, which depends on the bend allowance.
entries.explanation: The flat size changes with material, thickness, inside radius and K-factor. SOLIDWORKS computes it from the sheet-metal feature's settings.
entries.practice: Model as SOLIDWORKS sheet metal; put the flat pattern on the drawing (or supply it as DXF) with bend lines, directions and angles; state the K-factor or bend table used.
entries.example: 2 mm aluminium, inside radius 2, K-factor from the shop's bend table.
entries.correct: Flat pattern produced by SOLIDWORKS from the shop's bend data.
entries.mistake: Dimensioning only the formed part and letting the shop develop the blank.

entries.concept: Inside bend radius is set by material, thickness and tooling.
entries.explanation: Too small a radius cracks the material; the shop's tooling gives the radii it can make.
entries.practice: Use the shop's standard inside radius for the material and thickness; state it once in the notes.
entries.example: Mild steel 2 mm: inside radius 2 mm (confirm with the shop).
entries.correct: One standard radius, stated once.
entries.mistake: A different radius on every bend.

entries.concept: Holes too close to a bend distort when it is formed.
entries.explanation: A common shop rule keeps hole edges at least about 2 x thickness + inside radius from the bend; the shop's own rule wins.
entries.practice: Check hole positions against the bend lines; dimension formed features from the bend or the outside face the shop gauges from.
entries.example: 2 mm sheet, R2 bend: keep hole edges about 6 mm or more from the bend (rule of thumb).
entries.correct: Holes clear of bends, dimensioned from a gauged face.
entries.mistake: A hole straddling the bend line.

entries.concept: An assembly drawing shows how parts go together, not how each is made.
entries.explanation: It carries a bill of materials, balloons, overall sizes and only the dimensions needed to assemble or install.
entries.practice: Views that show every component; a balloon on each item; a BOM with item, part number, description, quantity; assembly notes (torques, adhesives) as specified.
entries.example: A shaft assembly: section through the shaft, balloons to bearings, circlips and housing.
entries.correct: BOM and balloons, few dimensions.
entries.mistake: Repeating detail dimensions of every part on the assembly.

entries.concept: Balloons point to each item once, neatly.
entries.explanation: Readers match balloons to BOM rows; crossing leaders and duplicates confuse them.
entries.practice: One balloon per item in the view that shows it best; leaders that do not cross; align balloons in rows or columns.
entries.example: Balloons arranged in a column to the right of the main view.
entries.correct: Every BOM item ballooned once; aligned.
entries.mistake: Auto-balloons scattered over the views with crossing leaders.

entries.concept: An exploded view shows assembly order and hidden parts.
entries.explanation: It is a pictorial aid for assembly and service, not for dimensions.
entries.practice: Explode along assembly axes in assembly order; balloon the parts; no dimensions.
entries.example: A pump: impeller, seal and cover exploded along the shaft axis.
entries.correct: Order of assembly visible.
entries.mistake: Random explode directions.

entries.concept: A spool drawing gives centre-line geometry between interfaces.
entries.explanation: Pipe fitters work to centre lines, flange faces and fitting take-outs; cut lengths follow from them.
entries.practice: Dimension centre line to centre line and to flange faces; list pipe, fittings and flanges with specification; show flange bolt-hole orientation.
entries.example: DN50 spool: 400 to the flange face, one long-radius elbow, flange holes straddling the vertical centre line.
entries.correct: Centre-line dimensions and a material list.
entries.mistake: Outside-of-pipe dimensions that ignore fitting take-outs.

entries.concept: Flange bolt holes straddle the centre lines unless stated.
entries.explanation: Two-hole-on-centre-line versus straddling decides whether mating flanges line up.
entries.practice: State the bolt-hole orientation for every flange; dimension the PCD, hole count and size from the flange standard and rating.
entries.example: 4 holes straddling the vertical and horizontal centre lines.
entries.correct: Orientation stated.
entries.mistake: Leaving orientation to chance.

entries.concept: Pressure equipment documentation follows the design code the owner names.
entries.explanation: Design pressure, temperature, materials, welding, NDT and testing are set by the applicable code and the designer; a drawing tool cannot decide them.
entries.practice: Ask which code applies; show only the requirements the designer states; mark the drawing as requiring the designer's verification.
entries.example: A spool for a pressure system: test pressure and NDT extent from the designer.
entries.correct: Code-driven requirements come from the designer.
entries.mistake: Assuming a code, rating or test pressure.

entries.concept: A general arrangement shows what the equipment is, where it goes and how it connects.
entries.explanation: Its readers plan space, foundations, lifting and connections: envelope, interfaces, masses and orientation matter; manufacturing detail does not.
entries.practice: Overall dimensions, interface positions, mounting and lifting points, access clearances, mass and centre of gravity when known.
entries.example: A pump skid GA: footprint, anchor holes, nozzle positions, lifting lugs, total mass.
entries.correct: Interfaces and envelope only.
entries.mistake: Detail dimensions of every part on the GA.

entries.concept: An installation drawing tells the installer how to fix and connect the item.
entries.explanation: Fixing pattern, foundation interface, clearances for service, connection points and handling instructions.
entries.practice: Dimension the fixing holes from the equipment's datum; state anchor type only if the designer specifies it; show service clearances.
entries.example: Anchor bolt pattern 1100 x 500 with service clearance 600 at the front.
entries.correct: Everything the installer needs on one sheet.
entries.mistake: No clearance or access information.

entries.concept: Lifting points and mass belong on the GA.
entries.explanation: Riggers need lift points, total mass and centre of gravity; lifting lug design is an engineering matter.
entries.practice: Show lifting points and state mass and centre of gravity when they are known from mass properties with real materials.
entries.example: Mass 850 kg (from SOLIDWORKS with materials assigned), CoG marked.
entries.correct: Masses from the model only when materials are assigned.
entries.mistake: Stating a mass computed without materials.

entries.concept: Each size and position is dimensioned once.
entries.explanation: Duplicates can disagree after a change; the reader cannot tell which is right.
entries.practice: Dimension each feature in one view only; use reference (bracketed) dimensions sparingly and only for information.
entries.example: Plate thickness in the edge view only.
entries.correct: No duplicates.
entries.mistake: The same length in two views.

entries.concept: A chain of dimensions plus the overall is over-dimensioned.
entries.explanation: With all segments and the overall dimensioned, tolerances cannot all be met; one dimension must be left out or shown as reference.
entries.practice: Leave out the least important segment, or dimension from one datum (baseline).
entries.example: A stepped shaft: lengths from one shoulder, the overall length, one step left out.
entries.correct: Open chain or baseline.
entries.mistake: Every step length and the overall length.

entries.concept: A hole is fully defined by one callout plus its position.
entries.explanation: The callout gives count, diameter, depth, counterbore or countersink and thread; the position comes from datums.
entries.practice: Use one leader callout per hole group (e.g. 6x Ø11 THRU, counterbore Ø17.5 depth 11); position the group from datums or by its pattern.
entries.example: 4x M6 depth 12, equally spaced on Ø80 pitch circle.
entries.correct: Complete callout, positioned from datums.
entries.mistake: A diameter only, with no depth or count.

entries.concept: Holes on a circle are dimensioned by the pitch circle diameter and angles.
entries.explanation: Giving x and y offsets of holes on a circle makes the reader compute the radius and hides the design intent.
entries.practice: Dimension the PCD, the hole count and spacing (equally spaced, or the angles), and the angular position of the first hole.
entries.example: 4x Ø5 on Ø80 PCD, equally spaced, first at 45°.
entries.correct: PCD and angles.
entries.mistake: 28.284 and 28.284 offsets for holes on a 40 mm radius.

entries.concept: Many holes in one face are clearer as ordinate dimensions or a hole table.
entries.explanation: Dozens of chained or baseline dimensions crowd the view; ordinates or a table give the same positions from one origin.
entries.practice: From about 8 holes, use ordinate dimensions from the datum corner, or tag holes and list them in a table.
entries.example: A mounting plate with 24 holes: hole table with X, Y and size per tag.
entries.correct: One origin, readable positions.
entries.mistake: Forty overlapping linear dimensions.

entries.concept: Geometric tolerances control form, orientation, location and runout when size tolerances cannot.
entries.explanation: They need a datum scheme and a reason: function or assembly. Applied without a reason they add cost.
entries.practice: Add feature control frames only where the designer specifies them; reference datums that exist on the drawing.
entries.example: Position of a bolt pattern relative to datums A, B, C, as specified.
entries.correct: Tolerances from the design, datums shown.
entries.mistake: Flatness and perpendicularity on every face 'to look professional'.

entries.concept: Runout controls how a turned diameter runs about the axis.
entries.explanation: Bearing journals and seals usually need it; the value comes from the bearing or seal maker and the designer.
entries.practice: Reference the common axis of the bearing diameters as datum; apply runout to diameters that rotate in contact, as specified.
entries.example: Seal diameter: circular runout to datum A-B (value from the designer).
entries.correct: Runout only where function needs it.
entries.mistake: Runout values guessed.

entries.concept: Datum features must be real, accessible surfaces.
entries.explanation: Inspectors and machinists must be able to touch or locate on them.
entries.practice: Choose datum features the part actually seats or locates on; label them with datum symbols.
entries.example: Datum A: the base face; B: the dowel hole.
entries.correct: Physical, functional datums.
entries.mistake: A model centre plane as a datum with no physical feature.

entries.concept: Mating diameters get a fit from the design: clearance, transition or interference.
entries.explanation: The fit decides how parts assemble and work (sliding, located, pressed). ISO 286 codes such as H7 for a hole express it.
entries.practice: Ask the designer for the fit at every seat, journal and locating bore; write it on the dimension (e.g. Ø52 H7).
entries.example: Bearing seat Ø52: fit from the bearing maker's recommendation, confirmed by the designer.
entries.correct: Fits stated where parts mate.
entries.mistake: A general tolerance on a bearing seat.

entries.concept: A general tolerance covers every dimension without its own tolerance.
entries.explanation: Without it, untoleranced dimensions have no limits and cannot be accepted or rejected. ISO 2768 classes (f, m, c, v) are common; the class is the designer's choice.
entries.practice: State the general tolerance once in the notes or title block; tolerance individually only what is tighter.
entries.example: GENERAL TOLERANCES: ISO 2768-m (when the designer confirms medium).
entries.correct: A general tolerance on every manufacturing drawing.
entries.mistake: No general tolerance, or one chosen by the drafting tool.

entries.concept: Tolerances add up along a chain.
entries.explanation: The worst case of a chain is the sum of its tolerances; dimensioning from one datum limits the stack.
entries.practice: Dimension functional relationships directly; check stacks across assemblies before tightening tolerances.
entries.example: Shaft shoulder to groove: given directly, not as the difference of two lengths from the end.
entries.correct: Direct dimension for the functional distance.
entries.mistake: Tightening every tolerance instead of re-dimensioning.

entries.concept: Surface texture is specified where function needs it, plus a general requirement.
entries.explanation: Sealing, sliding and bearing faces need a finish value; other faces follow a general note.
entries.practice: Put a surface texture symbol with the value on functional faces (when the designer gives it); state the general surface texture once.
entries.example: Seal journal Ra 0.4 (from the seal maker), general Ra 3.2.
entries.correct: Values from function or supplier data.
entries.mistake: The finest finish on every face.

entries.concept: Coatings and heat treatments change sizes and properties; state them and when sizes apply.
entries.explanation: Plating and paint add thickness; hardening can distort. The drawing says whether dimensions are before or after treatment.
entries.practice: State treatment and coating with their specification, and 'dimensions after plating' (or before) where it matters.
entries.example: Zinc plate (specification from the designer); dimensions apply after plating.
entries.correct: Treatment stated with its effect on sizes.
entries.mistake: Finish left to the shop.

entries.concept: Sharp edges are broken unless stated.
entries.explanation: A general note sets edge breaks; edges that must stay sharp (sealing, cutting) are marked.
entries.practice: One note: remove burrs and break sharp edges (size as the designer states); mark exceptions.
entries.example: BREAK SHARP EDGES 0.2-0.5 x 45° (when confirmed).
entries.correct: One general note, exceptions marked.
entries.mistake: A chamfer dimension on every edge.

entries.concept: Views are balanced on the sheet with room for dimensions.
entries.explanation: A crowded or lopsided sheet is hard to read; dimensions need space between views.
entries.practice: Place views in projection with gaps of about 20-30 mm for dimensions, the group balanced in the area above the title block, notes bottom left.
entries.example: A3 at 1:2 with 25 mm between views.
entries.correct: Balanced, aligned, readable.
entries.mistake: Views touching each other or the border.

entries.concept: Use a preferred scale that shows the part clearly on the smallest suitable sheet.
entries.explanation: Preferred scales (1:1, 1:2, 1:5, 2:1, 5:1...) are familiar; odd scales confuse.
entries.practice: Choose the largest preferred scale at which the views fit without crowding; enlarge small features with details rather than enlarging the whole part.
entries.example: A 300 x 200 plate: A3 at 1:2.
entries.correct: Preferred scale, details for small features.
entries.mistake: 1:1.7 to fill the sheet.

entries.concept: An isometric helps understanding but carries no dimensions.
entries.explanation: It is useful on assemblies, weldments and complex parts; on a simple plate or shaft it uses space for nothing.
entries.practice: Add an isometric when the shape is hard to read from orthographic views; keep it small, in a free corner, undimensioned.
entries.example: A weldment frame: small isometric top right.
entries.correct: Isometric only when it helps.
entries.mistake: Dimensions on the isometric.

entries.concept: Using a standard's symbols is not the same as complying with it.
entries.explanation: Compliance is a judgement by a qualified person against the current, licensed standard.
entries.practice: Name the conventions followed; leave compliance to the checker and approver.
entries.example: 'Drawn to AS 1100 conventions' rather than 'complies with AS 1100'.
entries.correct: Conventions named, compliance checked by a person.
entries.mistake: Claiming compliance because the projection symbol is right.

entries.concept: The title block identifies and controls the drawing.
entries.explanation: Title, drawing number, revision, material, finish, scale, projection, units, drawn, checked and approved with dates.
entries.practice: Fill every field the company template has; leave approval fields for the people who approve.
entries.example: BZ-1001, rev A, S355, drawn AB 08-11-2026, checked (blank until checked).
entries.correct: Complete identification; approvals by people.
entries.mistake: A drawing number missing, or an approval filled in by the tool.

entries.concept: Every change to a released drawing gets a new revision with a record.
entries.explanation: Workshops must know which revision is current and what changed.
entries.practice: Revision table with letter, description, date and approval; revision clouds or markers on changed areas when the company uses them.
entries.example: Rev C: counterbore depth 10 to 11.
entries.correct: Change recorded and approved.
entries.mistake: Changing a released drawing without a revision.

entries.concept: Critical dimensions are identified so inspection can focus on them.
entries.explanation: Inspection plans sample critical characteristics more often; the drawing marks them.
entries.practice: Mark critical dimensions as the company does (balloon numbers, a symbol or a table) once the designer confirms which are critical.
entries.example: Bearing seat diameter and PCD position marked critical.
entries.correct: Critical characteristics confirmed and marked.
entries.mistake: Every dimension marked critical.

entries.concept: A drawing is manufacturing-ready only after checking and approval.
entries.explanation: Saving a file proves nothing about its content. Tolerances, materials, threads, welds and notes must be confirmed, and a person releases the drawing.
entries.practice: Check, correct, re-check; release with an approval signature.
entries.example: QA report clear of blockers, then checked and approved by the engineer.
entries.correct: Human release after checks.
entries.mistake: Issuing a drawing because it saved without errors.

entries.concept: Dimension so the inspector can measure what is dimensioned.
entries.explanation: A depth to a hidden face or a position from an inaccessible point cannot be measured directly.
entries.practice: Dimension depths from accessible faces; positions from datums an inspector can locate on.
entries.example: Blind hole depth from the entry face.
entries.correct: Measurable dimensions.
entries.mistake: Depth from the far side of the part.

entries.concept: A typical clamp or mounting plate drawing.
entries.explanation: Synthetic illustrative example, not an approved drawing.
entries.practice: Plan view with hole positions from the centre lines or datum edges; edge view for thickness; section A-A through a counterbored hole and the stepped bore; hole callouts per group; PCD for holes on a circle; notes: units, general tolerance (confirmed), material, edge break.
entries.example: 300 x 200 x 25 plate, 6x counterbored holes, central stepped bore, 4 blind holes on a PCD.
entries.correct: Two views plus one section, grouped callouts.
entries.mistake: Three outside views and no section.

entries.concept: A typical turned shaft drawing.
entries.explanation: Synthetic illustrative example, not an approved drawing.
entries.practice: One side view with the axis horizontal, diameters on the steps, lengths from one shoulder, a detail of the groove at 5:1, a removed section at the cross hole; fits on journals as given by the designer.
entries.example: Ø30 / Ø40 / Ø30 shaft, 150 long, a circlip groove and a cross hole.
entries.correct: One view, one detail, one section.
entries.mistake: Front, top and right views of a round shaft.

entries.concept: A typical welded frame drawing.
entries.explanation: Synthetic illustrative example, not an approved drawing.
entries.practice: Plan and one elevation, small isometric, balloons to each member, cut list (section, length, end cuts, qty), weld symbols as specified, notes: welding standard and category (from the designer), finish.
entries.example: 500 x 300 frame in SHS 40x40x3.
entries.correct: Cut list and balloons; welds specified by the designer.
entries.mistake: No cut list; 'weld all joints'.

entries.concept: Mistake: dimensions to hidden lines.
entries.explanation: Hidden lines are hard to read and ambiguous.
entries.practice: Correction: add a section that shows the feature and dimension it there.
entries.example: Counterbore depth moved from the edge view's hidden lines to section A-A.
entries.correct: Section added.
entries.mistake: Dimension to a dashed line.

entries.concept: Mistake: information the reader must guess.
entries.explanation: Missing material, general tolerance, threads or welds stop production or cause scrap.
entries.practice: Correction: list every missing item and ask the designer before release; mark unknowns TO BE CONFIRMED on drafts.
entries.example: GENERAL TOLERANCES: TO BE CONFIRMED on a draft until the designer answers.
entries.correct: Unknowns visible, never filled with assumptions.
entries.mistake: A default tolerance or weld size chosen by the drafter.

entries.concept: Mistake: views that repeat other views.
entries.explanation: A third view of a plate shows the thickness again; an end view of a plain shaft shows a circle.
entries.practice: Correction: delete the view, or replace it with a section or detail that adds information.
entries.example: Right view of a plate removed; section A-A added.
entries.correct: Each view adds information.
entries.mistake: Default three-view layout kept.
